9750: Long, thin, and hanging limply — without fullness, bounce, or body.

1. Describing hair

This is where "lank" is used most often. Lank hair is straight, flat, and lifeless — it just hangs down without any volume, curl, or energy. Think of hair that lies completely flat against the head, perhaps slightly greasy or thin, with no bounce or movement to it. It doesn't wave, it doesn't curl, it doesn't lift. It simply droops.

"She pushed her lank hair away from her face."
"After hours in the rain, his hair hung in lank, wet strands."

The word suggests not just straightness but a kind of limpness — as if the hair has given up. It's slightly negative in tone. "Straight hair" is neutral; "lank hair" has a faint sense of dullness or neglect about it.

2. Describing a person or body part

When used for a person, "lank" means tall and thin — but in a way that looks somewhat ungainly or hollow, not in a graceful or athletic way. A lank person is thin to the point where their height makes them look stretched out and bony.

"A lank young man unfolded himself from the chair."
"His lank frame barely filled the oversized coat."

When used for specific body parts — fingers, limbs, a neck — it means long and thin, with a slightly lifeless or frail quality.

"She had lank, pale fingers that wrapped easily around the glass."

"Lank" always implies an absence of something — of fullness, of life, of vitality. Something lank is not robustly solid or richly textured. It is reduced, flat, thin. That's why it tends to carry a slightly melancholy or unflattering tone, even when used neutrally.

Compare it to related words:

  • Lean = simply thin (neutral, sometimes even admirable)
  • Lanky = tall and thin with an awkward, ungainly quality (very similar to lank for people — in fact, lanky comes from lank)
  • Limp = lacking stiffness or energy (focuses on limpness, not thinness)
  • Lank = the combination: thin and hanging limply, without body or energy
Lank means long and thin in a flat, lifeless, drooping way — most often describing hair that hangs without volume or curl, or a person/limb that is tall and thinly hollow-looking.
9751:
"Lanky" describes a person who is tall and thin, but in an ungainly, loose-limbed way. It is not just about being tall, and not just about being thin — it is the combination of both, along with a sense that the person's long limbs look a little awkward or loosely put together, like their body hasn't quite caught up with itself.

Think of a teenager who shot up several inches over a summer. Their arms hang a bit too long, their legs look spindly, and they move with a slightly clumsy, uncoordinated quality. That person is lanky.
Breaking it down: the three ingredients

When you call someone lanky, you are really pointing to three things at once:

  1. Tall — they are noticeably above average height.
  2. Thin — they have a slim, narrow build with little bulk or muscle.
  3. Loose or awkward-looking — their long limbs give them a slightly ungainly, poorly-coordinated appearance, as if their arms and legs are just a little too long for the rest of their body.

Remove any one of these and the word no longer fits perfectly. A short, thin person is not lanky. A tall, muscular person is not lanky. A tall, thin person who moves with great grace and elegance is usually not called lanky either.
The feeling of the word — its connotation

"Lanky" is a mildly informal and slightly negative word, though not cruelly so. It is more descriptive than insulting — something you might say affectionately, or casually, rather than as a sharp criticism.

It does carry a quiet implication of awkwardness. There is something a little unfinished or gawky about a lanky person — like a young foal whose legs are too long. It is often associated with adolescence, growth spurts, and that phase when a young person has not yet "grown into" their body.

That said, the word is not harsh. Saying "he is a lanky kid" is very different from saying something unkind. It is simply an honest, informal observation about how someone is built.
How it differs from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so here is a clear breakdown:

  • Slim / slender / lean — These just mean thin, and they are positive or neutral. A slim person looks elegant and well-proportioned. Lanky is different because it adds awkwardness and excessive height.
  • Gaunt — This means extremely thin in an unhealthy, hollow-cheeked way — almost sickly. Lanky does not imply illness; it just describes a tall, thin body type.
  • Gangly / gangling — These are the closest synonyms to lanky. They mean almost exactly the same thing: tall, thin, and awkward-looking. You can use them interchangeably in most sentences. "Gangly" perhaps emphasizes the awkward movement even more, but the difference is tiny.
  • Rangy — Similar again: tall and thin with long limbs. "Rangy" is slightly more neutral and is sometimes used positively (it can suggest athletic potential or a wiry toughness), whereas "lanky" leans more toward awkward.
  • Beanpole / string bean — These are informal or slang expressions for a very tall, thin person. They are more vivid and playful, and a bit more exaggerated.

The word is used almost exclusively for people, and occasionally for animals — a lanky young horse, a lanky dog with long legs.

It is most naturally applied to young people, especially teenagers, because the awkward-growth-spurt quality of the word fits that stage of life so well. But it can describe adults too — someone who has always had a tall, thin, loose-limbed build.

It is rarely (and only metaphorically) applied to objects or things.

• "The lanky teenager had to duck his head every time he walked through a doorway."
  • "She was lanky as a child but grew into a graceful, confident woman."
  • "The new basketball recruit was lanky but showed a lot of promise."
  • "A lanky figure in an oversized coat stood at the corner of the street."
  • "He had the lanky, loose-jointed look of someone who had grown six inches in one year."
Quick summary to lock it in

Lanky = tall + thin + awkward-looking, usually in a harmless, informal, slightly affectionate way. The image to hold in your mind is a young person with long arms, long legs, and a narrow frame — moving through the world in a slightly gawky, uncoordinated way, like their limbs arrived before the rest of them did.
9752: A lanyard is a strap or cord that you wear around your neck (or sometimes your wrist) to hold or carry a small object. Think of it as a wearable holder — it keeps something important close to your body and easy to reach, without you having to put it in a pocket or bag.

A lanyard is typically a flat, ribbon-like strip (or sometimes a round cord) about 45–60 cm long (roughly the distance from your shoulder to your waist), forming a loop that sits comfortably around your neck. At the bottom of this loop, there is usually a small metal or plastic clip or hook — this is where the object gets attached.

The strap itself is most commonly made from nylon, polyester, or cotton. It can be a plain single colour, or it can have text, logos, and patterns printed on it.

The whole point of a lanyard is to keep something dangling at chest level, visible and accessible. The most common things attached to a lanyard are:

  • ID cards or access badges — so employees, students, or event attendees can display their identity at all times
  • Keys — so you don't lose them
  • USB drives — small and easy to misplace otherwise
  • Whistles — very common for sports coaches, referees, and lifeguards
  • Small tools or devices — like a small torch or a camera
Where You'll See Lanyards in Real Life

The most familiar place is at offices and workplaces, where employees hang their ID badge from a lanyard so it's always visible. Security staff can simply glance at your chest to verify who you are.

At conferences, exhibitions, and events, every participant typically receives a lanyard with a name tag or entry pass attached — it's one of the first things handed to you at the registration desk.

At schools and universities, students often carry their ID cards on lanyards. In some institutions, wearing your ID on a lanyard is mandatory.

Sports environments are full of lanyards too — a referee's whistle almost always hangs from one.
An Important Feature: The Safety Breakaway

Many modern lanyards have a small breakaway clasp — a section near the back of the neck that snaps apart easily if the lanyard gets caught on something or is pulled sharply. This is a safety feature to prevent choking or injury. Once it snaps open, you can simply press the two pieces back together and it's re-connected. If you look closely at lanyards worn by hospital staff or factory workers, you'll almost always find this feature.

A common variation is the retractable lanyard, where the cord connecting the clip to the strap is coiled inside a small plastic housing. You can pull the card out to swipe it through a card reader, and the cord automatically retracts and pulls the card back when you let go. Office workers who need to tap their badge against a door scanner multiple times a day use these constantly.

While "lanyard" almost always brings to mind a neck strap, the word also covers straps worn around the wrist. A small loop of cord attached to a camera, a TV remote, a gaming controller, or a key — designed so the object doesn't fall and get damaged if you lose your grip — is also correctly called a lanyard. You'll see this wrist-loop version on most Nintendo controllers, ski poles, and professional cameras.
How It's Different from Similar Things

• A necklace is jewellery; a lanyard is a practical, functional tool.
  • A keychain attaches to a belt loop or sits in your pocket; a lanyard goes around the neck or wrist and keeps the object at chest level or in your hand.
  • A badge holder is just the clear plastic sleeve that holds the card; the lanyard is the strap that the badge holder clips onto.
A lanyard is a strap or cord worn around the neck or wrist, fitted with a clip at one end, used to hold and display objects like ID cards, keys, or whistles so they are always accessible and visible.
9753:
"Lap" has three distinct meanings as a noun, plus important idioms. Here is each one explained fully.

Meaning 1 — The flat surface your thighs form when you sit

This is by far the most common meaning. When you sit down, your upper legs (thighs) become roughly flat and horizontal, creating a natural upward-facing surface. That surface is your lap.

Think of it as a shelf your own body makes when you sit.

  • "The cat curled up in his lap."
  • "She balanced the book on her lap."
  • "He accidentally spilled soup on his lap."

One crucial detail: your lap exists only when you are sitting. The moment you stand up, it disappears. You would never say "the cat is sitting in my lap" while standing — it wouldn't make sense, because there's no lap to sit in.

The lap also carries a strong sense of closeness and comfort. When a small child sits "in someone's lap," the child is sitting on that person's thighs, nestled against their body. It is an intimate, nurturing position, which is why laps are associated with warmth and care.

This is also why a portable computer is called a laptop — it is designed to rest on your lap while you sit. And a lapdog is a dog small enough to sit comfortably on your lap. (The word "lapdog" is also used figuratively for a person who blindly follows and obeys another — "He's the manager's lapdog.")

Meaning 2 — One complete circuit or length (in sports and racing)

In running, cycling, motor racing, and similar sports, a lap is one complete trip around a track — starting from a point and returning to that exact same point, having gone all the way around.

  • "The race is 20 laps long." → The cars circle the track 20 full times.
  • "She completed 8 laps before stopping." → She ran around the oval track 8 times.
  • "He's leading after lap 15." → He is in first place 15 circuits into the race.

In swimming, a lap typically means one length of the pool — swimming from one wall to the other. However, some people (especially in casual use) use "lap" to mean going down and coming back, which would be two lengths. Both usages exist in real life; context usually makes it clear which one is meant.

This meaning is also used loosely and figuratively to describe a stage or stretch of any journey or long task:

  • "We're on the final lap of this project." → We're almost done.
  • "The last lap of the road trip was the most tiring." → The final stretch of the drive.

Meaning 3 — An overlapping section (technical use)

When one flat piece of material is laid on top of another so that one extends over the edge of the other, that overlapping area is called a lap. You will encounter this mainly in construction, carpentry, roofing, and sewing.

  • "The roof shingles have a three-inch lap." → Each shingle overlaps the one below it by three inches, so rain cannot get through the gap.
  • A lap joint in woodworking is a connection where two pieces of wood are joined by each overlapping the other.

This is a specialized, technical meaning. You won't hear it in ordinary conversation, but it is a real and established sense of the word.

A word's full meaning includes the fixed phrases it appears in. These three are important and widely used:

"In the lap of luxury"
Living in great comfort, surrounded by wealth and ease.

  • "They spent the holiday in the lap of luxury."

The image is of being cradled and held by luxury itself, as if sitting in its lap.

"In the lap of the gods"
Something whose outcome is uncertain and completely outside human control — left to fate or chance.

  • "The final score is in the lap of the gods now."
  • "Whether the treatment works is in the lap of the gods."

The idea is that the matter has been handed over to a higher power, and humans can do nothing more about it.

"Fall / drop into someone's lap"
Something comes to a person easily and without effort on their part — they didn't have to seek it out or work for it; it simply arrived.

  • "She wasn't even looking for a job — the offer just fell into her lap."
  • "Opportunities don't usually drop into your lap; you have to go after them."

On your bodyThe flat surface your thighs create when you sit; exists only when seated
In sport/racingOne complete circuit around a track, or one length of a swimming pool
In constructionThe area where one piece of material overlaps another

Those are all the core senses of "lap" as a noun — the body sense, the racing sense, the technical/overlap sense — plus the three most important idioms built around it.
9754:
A lapdog is a small, domestic pet dog — one that is tiny enough to sit comfortably on a person's lap. These dogs are typically kept purely for companionship. They don't guard homes or herd sheep. They just sit close to their owner, follow them around, and do whatever the owner pleases. They are pampered, gentle, and completely dependent on the person who keeps them.

Think of a tiny, fluffy dog sitting on a wealthy person's lap, being fed treats and stroked all day. That image is the foundation of this word.

In everyday language, "lapdog" is almost always used figuratively — and this is the meaning you'll encounter most often.

When you call a person a lapdog, you mean they behave exactly like that small pet dog: they are completely obedient, eager to please, and entirely controlled by someone more powerful. They do whatever that powerful person wants, without question, without pushback, and without any independent thought or backbone.

A lapdog person:

  • Agrees with everything their superior says, even when it is wrong
  • Never challenges or questions the person they serve
  • prioritizes pleasing that person over doing what is right
  • Allows themselves to be used and directed as a tool
  • Has essentially surrendered their own will and judgment

The key idea is total, uncritical submission to a more powerful person or group.
The Tone: It Is Always an Insult

Calling someone a lapdog is deeply insulting. It is not a neutral description. It is a criticism that attacks a person's dignity, independence, and integrity all at once.

When you use this word, you are saying:

  • This person has no spine.
  • This person thinks for themselves not at all.
  • This person is owned by someone else, the way a pet is owned.
  • This person is being used and is too weak — or too self-interested — to resist it.

The insult stings because it compares a human being to a pet animal. It strips away their dignity and their agency.

This word is used most often in politics, business, journalism, and international affairs — anywhere that power dynamics exist between people or institutions.

In politics:
If a politician always votes however their party leader tells them to, never standing up for their own voters or conscience, people will call them the party's lapdog.

In the media:
If a newspaper or TV channel consistently defends a powerful politician no matter what that politician does — never reporting critically, always framing things favorably — critics might call that outlet the politician's lapdog.

In the workplace:
If an employee agrees with every single thing their boss says, never offering an honest opinion, always laughing at the boss's jokes and praising their decisions even when bad, colleagues might privately call that person the boss's lapdog.

In international relations:
If a smaller or weaker country consistently supports a more powerful country's foreign policy without any independent judgment — voting with them at the United Nations, echoing their positions automatically — political commentators may call the weaker country the other's lapdog.

The entire meaning of this word rests on one image: a small, harmless pet dog that sits on its owner's lap, completely dependent, completely obedient, and perfectly content to be controlled.

When applied to a person, you are saying: this person is not truly independent — they belong to someone more powerful, and they act like it.
Subtle Shade of Meaning: It Implies Willingness

This is a detail worth noting. A lapdog is not someone who is forced into submission against their will. A lapdog chooses this role — often because they gain something from it: protection, status, money, access to power, or simply approval.

This is part of what makes the insult so sharp. The lapdog isn't a victim. They have made a choice to surrender their independence, and that choice is seen as a moral failing — a sign of weakness, selfishness, or cowardice.

LiteralA small pet dog kept on one's lap
FigurativeA person who is completely obedient and subservient to someone powerful, with no independent will
ToneStrongly negative; an insult
ImpliesLack of independence, dignity, and backbone; a willingness to be controlled
Common contextsPolitics, media, business, international relations

• "The senator has become nothing more than a lapdog for the oil industry — he votes against every environmental bill they dislike."
  • "The newspaper was once respected, but it's now the prime minister's lapdog, printing whatever the government wants people to believe."
  • "He was tired of being the CEO's lapdog — agreeing with everything, never being heard — so he finally quit."

That is the full picture of "lapdog." The literal dog-on-a-lap image gives you the root; every figurative use of the word is simply that same image applied to a person who has made themselves into someone else's obedient, spineless, and willing servant.
9755: A lapel is the folded-back flap of fabric on the front of a jacket or coat, on either side of your chest.

Put on a suit jacket or a blazer. Now look at the front. Below the collar and above the first button, there is a triangular (or sometimes curved) flap of fabric that folds outward and lies flat against your chest — one on the left side, one on the right. That folded flap is the lapel. Together, the two sides are called "lapels" (plural).

The lapel is not a pocket, not the collar, and not a separate piece sewn on. It is the same fabric as the jacket, but folded back over itself to create a layered, neat-looking flap.---

The lapel has two visible edges:

  • The outer edge, which curves or angles outward toward your shoulder.
  • The inner edge, where the lapel meets the collar. This meeting point creates a small notch or V-shape, which is one of the most recognizable features of a classic suit.

The lapel sits flat, smooth, and neat — it is not sticking out. It folds back gently, almost like a page of a book turned over.
The three shapes lapels come in

Lapels are not all the same shape. There are three main types:

  1. Notched lapel — The most common one. Where the lapel meets the collar, there is a small triangular cut-out (a "notch"). You see this on everyday business suits, blazers, and casual jackets.
  2. Peaked lapel — The outer tip of the lapel points sharply upward toward the shoulder, creating a more dramatic, angular look. This is considered more formal and is common on tuxedos and double-breasted suits.
  3. Shawl lapel — There is no notch at all. The lapel flows in one smooth, rounded curve from one side of the collar all the way around. This is the most elegant and is mostly found on dinner jackets and tuxedos.
The small hole on the lapel

Most suit jackets have a small vertical buttonhole on the left lapel (on your left when you are wearing it). This hole has a specific purpose: to hold a boutonnière — a small flower or decorative plant worn on formal occasions like weddings. This hole is called a lapel buttonhole or boutonnière hole.

A lapel pin is a small decorative pin — often made of metal — that people attach to their lapel as a personal or symbolic accessory. You might see country flags, company logos, causes, or decorative designs worn this way. It attaches by a pin at the back, poking through the fabric of the lapel.
What kind of clothes have lapels?

Lapels appear on:

  • Suit jackets and blazers
  • Overcoats and trench coats
  • Tuxedos and dinner jackets
  • Some cardigans and structured casual jackets

You will not find a lapel on T-shirts, hoodies, or most casual tops. The lapel is a feature of structured, tailored garments.

You'll often come across the word lapel in descriptions of physical actions:

  • Someone grabs another person "by the lapels" — meaning they grab the front of their jacket, one hand on each flap, as a threatening or dramatic gesture.
  • A tailor "presses the lapels" — flattening them neatly with an iron.
  • Someone "pins a flower to their lapel" — attaching a boutonnière for a formal event.

• He straightened his tie and smoothed down his lapels before walking into the interview.
  • She grabbed him by the lapels and pulled him closer.
  • The general wore several medals on his left lapel.
  • The tailor sewed a silk lining on the inside of the lapels.
  • A simple peaked lapel gives a suit a sharper, more formal look.
One-line summary to remember it forever
A lapel is the folded-back flap of fabric on the front of a jacket or coat — the triangular part that lies flat on your chest on either side, below the collar and above the buttons.
9756:
The adjective "lapidary" has a literal sense and a much more widely used figurative sense. You need both to fully own this word.

Literally, it means relating to the cutting, polishing, and engraving of precious stones and gems. A lapidary technique, for example, is one used to shape or finish a gemstone. This literal sense is straightforward and not where the word gets interesting.

Figuratively — and this is the sense you will encounter most often — lapidary describes writing, language, or expression that is refined, precise, and perfectly polished, with not a single word wasted. Think of it as the verbal equivalent of a flawlessly cut gem: compact, hard-edged, brilliantly clear, and built to last.

To truly feel what "lapidary" means, picture a stone engraver carving words into a monument. He cannot be sloppy. He cannot ramble. Every letter costs effort and space. So he must choose words that are short, exact, and powerful enough to outlast centuries. The result is language that has been cut down and polished until it is almost geometrically perfect.

When someone calls a piece of writing lapidary, they are paying it a very specific compliment. They mean it has these qualities all at once:

Conciseness. There is no flab, no filler, no digression. Every single word is earning its place.

Precision. The words don't approximately say what the writer means — they exactly say it. There is no vagueness or blur.

Polish. The sentences feel finished. They have a smooth, deliberate quality, as if they went through many rounds of careful refinement. You can sense the craft in them.

Weight and permanence. Lapidary writing feels like it could be engraved on a wall and read a hundred years from now. It has a timeless solidity to it.

All four qualities together, in one word: lapidary.

Here are sentences where "lapidary" is used correctly, followed by an explanation of why it fits:

"Hemingway's prose is lapidary — short sentences, zero decoration, every word doing real work."

Here it means his style is stripped down and polished to perfection. There is nothing loose or excessive about it.

"She ended her speech with a lapidary line that the audience remembered for years."

One perfectly crafted, compact sentence — precise and memorable, like something carved in stone.

"The ancient inscription was lapidary in both the literal and figurative sense: cut into marble, and composed with absolute economy of language."

A nice example of both meanings overlapping at once.

"Critics praised the novelist's lapidary sentences but admitted the book felt cold."

This is important — it hints that lapidary is not always a purely warm compliment. Precision and polish, taken to an extreme, can feel austere or even emotionally distant. The word acknowledges craft without necessarily implying warmth.

It does not mean simply "short." A tweet can be short without being lapidary. Lapidary implies that the brevity is achieved through skill — that a less careful writer would have needed far more words to say the same thing, and even then wouldn't have said it as well.

It does not mean "simple." Lapidary writing can carry complex ideas. What makes it lapidary is that those complex ideas are expressed with maximum efficiency and elegance, not that the ideas themselves are easy.

It does not mean "beautiful" in a lush or flowery way. In fact, it often implies the opposite — a spare, disciplined beauty, not an ornate one. If writing is lapidary, it is closer to a diamond than to a garden.

"Lapidary" is a formal, literary word. You will encounter it in book reviews, literary criticism, essays about writing style, and in serious newspapers. It is used by people who talk carefully about language. Using it yourself signals that you are thinking precisely about how something is written, not just what it says.

If you want to boil the whole adjective down to its essence:

Lapidary means so carefully and precisely crafted — with nothing unnecessary left in — that the language feels polished, weighty, and permanent, like words engraved in stone.

Hold onto that image — the stone engraver who cannot afford a wasted word — and you will never misuse or misunderstand this word again.
9757: At the heart of every meaning of lapse is a single idea: something slipping away from where it should be — either a standard slips, time slips, or a right/agreement slips away. Once you feel this central image, all the meanings of the word will make sense to you naturally.
Meaning 1: A Temporary Failure or Slip-Up

This is the most everyday meaning. A lapse is a small, usually brief failure to maintain a standard you normally keep — in behaviour, judgment, memory, or attention. It is almost always unintentional, which is what separates it from a deliberate wrongdoing.

The key word here is temporary. A lapse is a momentary slip, not a permanent character flaw or a pattern. It implies that the person is generally capable and responsible, but something slipped just this once.

Examples:

  • A doctor who is normally extremely careful makes a small error in a prescription. That is a lapse in judgment.
  • A student who always pays attention in class suddenly zones out for a few minutes. That is a lapse in concentration.
  • You forget the name of someone you have known for years. That is a lapse in memory (or a memory lapse).
  • A recovering alcoholic who had stayed sober for months drinks one night. That single episode is called a lapse.

Notice the tone: a lapse carries a sense of disappointment but not condemnation. It's a slip, not a sin.
Meaning 2: A Slip Back Into a Bad or Lower State

Closely related to Meaning 1, a lapse can also describe the act of sliding back into something negative — a bad habit, a worse condition, or a lower standard — after a period of having avoided it or done better.

Examples:

  • After years of good financial discipline, he had a lapse into reckless spending.
  • The country had a lapse into chaos after the peace talks broke down.
  • She had maintained her diet for months, but the holidays brought a lapse into old eating habits.

Think of it like a person walking uphill who loses their footing and slides back down a few steps. They haven't fallen to the bottom — it's a slip backward, not a total collapse.
Meaning 3: A Period of Time Passing

A lapse can simply mean a stretch or interval of time that has passed, especially between two events. This meaning is neutral — it carries no sense of failure. It just refers to time that has gone by.

Examples:

  • After a lapse of ten years, the two old friends finally met again.
  • There was a lapse of several seconds before anyone responded.
  • The discovery was made after a lapse of three decades since the original research.

In this meaning, "lapse" highlights the gap or passage of time rather than what happened during it. You'll often see the phrase "after a lapse of [time]" or "a time lapse" (though "time-lapse" in photography is a slightly specialised use of this same idea — capturing change over a long period of time by compressing it).
Meaning 4: The Ending of a Right, Agreement, or Privilege Due to Neglect or Inaction

In more formal contexts — especially in law, insurance, and business — a lapse means the termination or expiry of something (a right, a policy, a contract, an offer) because the required action was not taken in time, or because it simply was not renewed or maintained.

This is not a dramatic cancellation. It is a quiet, gradual expiry — something slipping away because nobody kept it alive.

Examples:

  • If you stop paying your insurance premiums, your policy will suffer a lapse — it quietly ceases to be valid.
  • A legal right can be lost through a lapse if it is not exercised within the required time period.
  • The offer was good for 48 hours, and after that time passed without a response, it ended in a lapse.
  • A passport that has not been renewed has lapsed — you can refer to the event of it becoming invalid as a lapse.

The key feature here is passivity — a lapse in this sense happens because someone failed to act, not because someone actively cancelled or destroyed something. Time ran out. The thing slipped away quietly.
The Single Thread Connecting All Meanings

Look at all four meanings again:

MeaningWhat slips away
A failure in attention or behaviourA standard slips
A slide back into something badProgress slips backward
A period of time passingTime slips by
Expiry of a right or agreementA privilege slips away

In every single case, something that was being held or maintained has slipped — either briefly, gradually, or permanently. That is the soul of the word.
Degree and Weight of a Lapse

One important nuance: a lapse is almost always minor to moderate in severity. It is rarely used for catastrophic or total failures. This is partly what makes the word useful — it signals a problem while simultaneously suggesting the problem is containable.

  • Forgetting to call your friend back = a lapse. ✓
  • Betraying a country's secrets over many years = not a lapse. ✗

Similarly, a lapse is often forgivable in tone. When you describe something as a lapse, you are usually implying that the person is better than this one incident, and that recovery is possible.

These are the most natural and frequently used combinations with "lapse" that you will encounter:

  • A lapse in concentration / attention / focus — a moment of losing mental focus
  • A lapse in judgment — a poor decision made in a moment of weakness or confusion
  • A memory lapse — a temporary failure to remember something
  • A lapse in security — a failure in a protective system or process
  • A moral lapse — a failure to act according to one's own ethical standards
  • An ethical lapse — similar to a moral lapse, often used in professional contexts
  • A time lapse — the passing of a significant period of time
  • A policy lapse — the expiry of an insurance or other formal policy
  • A lapse into silence / unconsciousness / bad habits — a sliding back or falling into a state

Lapse vs. Mistake: A mistake is simply an error. A lapse has the added idea of slipping from a standard — it implies there was a proper level that was not maintained. All lapses involve a kind of mistake, but not all mistakes are lapses.

Lapse vs. Relapse: A relapse is stronger and more complete — it means fully falling back into a bad state (especially illness or addiction). A lapse is smaller and more temporary. A relapse is often built from a lapse that was not caught in time.

Lapse vs. Lapse of time vs. Gap: When talking about time, a gap is simply an empty space. A lapse of time has a slightly more reflective or literary feel — it often implies you are aware of how much time has quietly slipped by.

A lapse is a slip — whether it's a slip in your behaviour, a slip backward into something bad, time slipping quietly by, or a right slipping away from you because it wasn't maintained. It is a word that lives in the territory between "everything is fine" and "serious failure." It names those quiet, often regrettable moments when something that was being held... wasn't held quite tightly enough.
9758:
At the heart of "lapse" is one simple picture: something that was once active, strong, or valid slowly slipping away — fading, expiring, or falling into a worse condition.

Think of it like a flame quietly dying out. It doesn't explode. It doesn't get switched off. It just... gradually stops being what it was. That slow, quiet slipping is what "lapse" captures.

"Lapse" as a verb carries a few closely related meanings. They all share the same soul — that idea of quiet slipping — but apply in different situations.

1. To slip or fall into a worse or different state

This is the most common use. When someone (or something) lapses into something, they gradually move from one state into another — usually a worse, weaker, or less desirable one.

The word "into" is your strongest clue that this meaning is being used.

Examples:

  • She lapsed into silence after hearing the news. — She gradually stopped talking and became silent.
  • He lapsed into his old bad habits after quitting therapy. — He slowly fell back into behaviors he had previously given up.
  • The patient lapsed into a coma overnight. — The patient's condition gradually worsened into unconsciousness.
  • The conversation lapsed into meaningless small talk. — The quality of the conversation slowly deteriorated.
  • After moving back to his hometown, he lapsed into the local dialect again. — He naturally and gradually slipped back into speaking the way he used to.

Notice: the slipping is never sudden. It's gradual, almost effortless — like water finding the lowest ground.

2. To become no longer valid because of inaction or the passage of time

This is the formal and legal use of the word. When a contract, membership, license, subscription, insurance policy, or right lapses, it means it has expired or become invalid — not because someone cancelled it, but because it was not renewed, maintained, or claimed in time.

The key distinction here: the person didn't actively end it. They simply let it slide, and time did the rest.

Examples:

  • His passport has lapsed — he forgot to renew it. — The passport is no longer valid.
  • Her gym membership lapsed after she stopped paying the monthly fee. — The membership quietly expired due to non-payment.
  • The insurance policy lapsed because no one renewed it. — The policy is no longer active.
  • The copyright lapsed, so the book is now free for anyone to publish.
  • Their agreement lapsed after two years with no renegotiation.

Think of it this way: if you actively cancel something, you ended it. If it lapses, time ended it — because you did nothing.

3. To temporarily fail to maintain a standard, discipline, or principle

Here, "lapse" is used when someone briefly slips up — when they fail, just for a moment, to live up to a standard they normally hold. It's a temporary failure, not a permanent one.

This use suggests a single slip, not a complete giving up.

Examples:

  • He lapsed in his diet and ate a whole pizza. — He briefly broke his diet rules.
  • Even the best professionals lapse occasionally. — Even skilled people make temporary mistakes.
  • She lapsed in judgment and trusted the wrong person. — She temporarily failed to think clearly.
  • The doctor lapsed in his duty by not checking the records carefully.

The important nuance: a lapse here is a crack, not a collapse. The person still upholds the standard most of the time. It's a temporary slip, not a permanent change of character.

4. To pass (said of time)

In this use, "lapse" simply means that time has gone by or elapsed. It's a slightly formal or literary way of saying time has passed.

Examples:

  • Several years lapsed before they spoke again. — Several years passed.
  • Only a few minutes had lapsed when the alarm went off.
  • Much time has lapsed since the original agreement was made.

You'll notice this meaning connects to the noun phrase "time-lapse" — a technique where time is made to appear as if it has passed very quickly.

Every use of "lapse" as a verb shares this: something that existed — a state, a validity, a standard, or time itself — quietly slips away or deteriorates without force or drama.

  • A person lapses into something (a state, silence, old habits).
  • A document or membership lapses (becomes invalid).
  • A standard or discipline lapses (temporarily fails).
  • Time lapses (passes).

"Lapse into" vs "relapse into"
Both mean to fall back into a worse state, but there's a difference in intensity. Relapse suggests falling back specifically after a period of recovery (especially in the context of illness or addiction). Lapse is broader and more general — it doesn't require any previous recovery period.

  • He relapsed into addiction after three years of sobriety. (He had recovered; now he's back.)
  • She lapsed into her old study habits as the semester got busier. (No recovery implied — just a general return.)

"Lapse" is passive by nature
Nobody forces a lapse. It happens through inaction, neglect, or the quiet pull of old patterns. This is what separates it from words like fall, drop, or descend, which can feel more sudden or dramatic. A lapse is always gradual, quiet, almost unnoticed until it has already happened.

To lapse means to gradually slip — into a worse state, into inactivity, into expiration, or into a temporary failure — through a process that is quiet, slow, and often driven more by neglect or the passage of time than by any deliberate action.
9759:
Larcenous means of, relating to, characterized by, or involving theft. It is the adjective form of the noun larceny, which is the legal term for the deliberate, wrongful taking of someone else's property with the intention of keeping it permanently. So when you attach the word "larcenous" to something, you are saying it has the quality, nature, or character of theft.

Think of it this way: larceny is the crime, and larcenous is the word that says something belongs to or smells like that crime.
What Can Be Described as Larcenous?

The word is flexible — it can describe a person, an action, an intention, or a scheme.

A person. Calling someone larcenous means they are thieving by nature, habit, or tendency. It paints them as someone whose character is that of a thief — someone with a constant impulse or history of stealing.

"The larcenous pickpocket worked his way through the crowded marketplace."

An act or behavior. An action is larcenous if it constitutes theft or is built around stealing.

"The employee's larcenous behavior — pocketing cash from the register — went unnoticed for months."

An intention or motive. In legal language especially, the phrase larcenous intent is very important. It refers to the deliberate, conscious purpose of stealing — meaning the person knew the property wasn't theirs and meant to permanently take it anyway. Without this intent, the act may not legally qualify as larceny at all.

"The defense argued that there was no larcenous intent — the defendant genuinely believed the bicycle was abandoned."

A plan or scheme. Any plot or strategy designed around stealing can be called larcenous.

"They devised a larcenous scheme to siphon funds from the company over several years."
The Figurative Use — When Nothing Is Actually Stolen

Beyond its strict, legal meaning, larcenous is also used figuratively in everyday language to describe something that feels like robbery — usually because of extreme unfairness, exploitation, or outrageous pricing. In this use, no actual crime is taking place, but the speaker is dramatizing how unjust or excessive something is.

"Those ticket service fees are absolutely larcenous!"
"The hotel charged a larcenous amount for a tiny bottle of water."

This figurative use is common and completely acceptable. It adds sharpness and color to language. When someone calls a price "larcenous," they mean it's so unreasonably high that it might as well be theft.
An Important Distinction — What Larcenous Does NOT Imply

This is where the razor-sharp accuracy matters.

Larcenous does not mean violent. Larceny is specifically a non-violent crime. The moment theft involves physical force, threats, or intimidation against a person, it becomes robbery — a different and more serious crime. Larcenous, therefore, carries no implication of violence or physical confrontation. It is purely about taking what isn't yours.

Larcenous does not mean accidental. The idea of intention is built into the word. If someone genuinely mistakes another person's umbrella for their own and walks off with it, that is not larcenous — there was no intent to steal. Larcenous always implies a knowing, deliberate act of taking.
The Scale of the Theft Doesn't Change the Word

Larceny legally comes in two broad degrees — petty larceny (small-scale theft, like stealing a phone) and grand larceny (large-scale theft, like stealing a car or a large sum of money). The adjective larcenous applies equally to both ends of the scale. Whether the theft is trivial or enormous, the word larcenous can describe it without any change in meaning.

• Larceny (noun) — the act of theft itself: "He was charged with grand larceny."
  • Larcenously (adverb) — in a thieving manner: "She larcenously helped herself to her colleague's credit card details."
The Complete Picture in One Sentence

Larcenous describes anything — a person, an action, a plan, or a motive — that is characterized by deliberate, non-violent theft, or that resembles theft in its unfairness; and figuratively, it describes anything so outrageously excessive that it feels like stealing.
